chapters.short: The dictionary form, the five decisions every verb makes, and how to read the two headwords in a pair.

sets.title: What a verb decides
sets.ask: Pick what the question is about

items.q: Which of these is the dictionary form (bezokolicznik) of the verb meaning "to write"?
items.why: pisać is the infinitive — the form you look up and learn. The others are used forms: pisanie-type forms are nouns, piszę is "I write", pisałem is "I wrote", pisze is "he writes".

items.q: How many tenses does Polish have?
items.why: Present, past and future. English has more shapes (I write, I am writing, I have written, I will have been writing), but Polish puts most of that meaning into aspect, not into extra tenses.

items.q: Which of these tells you the aspect of a verb?
opts: Its ending in the dictionary form
Whether the dictionary marks it impf or pf
The tense it is used in
items.a: Whether the dictionary marks it impf or pf
items.why: Aspect is a property of the verb itself, not of the sentence: every verb is either imperfective or perfective, and a dictionary says which with impf/pf or ndk./dk. The infinitive ending hints at the family it belongs to, but it does not decide aspect.

items.q: You look up "buy" and find kupić. What should you write down?
items.why: Learn both halves of the pair as one item. kupować is the process, kupić is the finished act. Learning one half is the most common way to learn a verb wrong — chapter 2 is entirely about this.

items.q: In a Polish past-tense form like pisałem, what does the ending show that English "I wrote" does not?
items.why: pisałem (male speaker) versus pisałam (female speaker). Polish past-tense forms carry gender, so the speaker's sex is never hidden.

items.q: Which ending is not a possible Polish infinitive ending?
items.why: -ć (pisać), -c (móc) and -ść (iść) all occur. -æ is not a Polish letter or ending at all.

sets.title: Reading the infinitive
sets.ask: What family does the ending point to?

items.q: czytać ends in -ać. What is its present tense likely to look like?
items.why: The -ać family overwhelmingly goes to -am, -asz: czytać → czytam, mieszkać → mieszkam, pytać → pytam. It is the largest family in the language.

items.q: mówić ends in -ić. What is its present tense likely to look like?
items.why: The -ić family goes to -ię, -isz: mówić → mówię, mówisz; robić → robię, robisz; dzwonić → dzwonię, dzwonisz.

items.q: Which of these verbs is perfective?
items.why: napisać is perfective — the finished act of writing. pisać and czytać are imperfective. piec means "to bake" and is imperfective too.

items.q: Which of these is a legitimate way to translate szukać?
items.why: szukać is to look for, an ongoing search, and it takes the genitive. To find is znaleźć, its perfective partner — a different word, and that difference matters (chapter 2).

items.q: A verb marked pf in a dictionary has:
items.why: A perfective verb describes a completed act, and something already complete cannot be happening now. Its present-looking forms are the future: napisać → napiszę = "I will write".
być — the most irregular verb in the language, and the one you cannot avoid (chapter 8).
mieć — a -m, -sz verb: mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają.

sets.title: Transitive or not?
sets.ask: Does it take a direct object?

items.q: Czytam ___ — "I am reading a book". Which case is book in?
items.why: czytać is transitive and takes a plain direct object: the accusative. Czytam książkę. Note that a negation would turn it genitive: Nie czytam książki.

items.q: Szukam ___ — "I am looking for the keys". Which case?
items.why: szukać takes the genitive even though English "look for" takes a plain object. The case is a property of the verb, not of the English translation — this is rekcja, chapter 9.

items.q: Pomagam ___ — "I am helping my mum". Which case?
items.why: pomagać takes the dative: Pomagam mamie. The person helped is the receiver of the help, and the receiver is the dative's job.
The object of mieć is accusative (bilet), but negating a verb turns that object into the genitive: nie mam biletu. This rule is so reliable that Polish teachers call it the negation genitive.

items.q: Which is the better translation of Znam Łódź.?
items.why: znać = to know a person, a place or a language — familiarity. wiedzieć = to know a fact. You znasz Łódź but wiesz, where the station is.

items.q: Which of these verbs is intransitive?
items.why: iść (to go on foot) takes no direct object; it takes a destination with a preposition: Idę do sklepu (do + genitive), Idę na koncert (na + accusative).

items.q: Someone says Kupuję chleb when they mean "I'll buy the bread (now, once)". What went wrong?
opts: They used the imperfective where the perfective is meant
items.a: They used the imperfective where the perfective is meant
items.why: For a single, completed purchase you want the perfective kupię: Kupię chleb. Kupuję describes a process or a habit — "I buy bread (regularly)" or "I'm in the middle of buying it". The case was fine; the aspect was not.

items.q: Why does Ja to zrobię sound different from To zrobię?
opts: The pronoun adds emphasis — "it's me who'll do it"
items.a: The pronoun adds emphasis — "it's me who'll do it"
items.why: Polish endings already say who does it, so an added pronoun is a choice: it stresses the person. To zrobię is neutral; ja to zrobię says "I'll do it, not you".

items.q: Someone wants to say "I am writing" using napisać. Why can't they?
opts: napisać is perfective and has no present tense
items.a: napisać is perfective and has no present tense
items.why: A completed act cannot be happening now. napiszę is the future: "I will write (and it will be written)". For "I am writing", use the imperfective: piszę.

items.q: What is the difference between Piszę list and Napiszę list?
items.why: Piszę — I am writing / I write, the process. Napiszę — I will write it and it will be done, the result. The same root, the same object, a different claim about completion.

chapters.short: Imperfective and perfective: the one distinction that shapes the whole verb. Learn to see both halves of a pair.

items.why: It has a completing prefix na- and no present tense: napiszę is the future. Its partner is pisać.
The longer, -ować form is the process — "to buy, to be buying". Its perfective partner is the shorter kupić.
z- is the plainest completing prefix in Polish. zrobię = I will do it, and it will be done. Partner: robić.
czytać is reading as a process, and it takes the accusative object książkę. Its perfective partner is przeczytać — to read it through.
prze- = through: to read something from start to finish. Przeczytam tę książkę = I'll read this book (all of it).
One completed taking. Wezmę is the future. Its imperfective partner is a completely different word, brać — a suppletive pair.
Speaking as an ongoing activity. The perfective partner is powiedzieć — to say something, one completed statement.
Powiem = I will say it. It is one finished statement, not the business of speaking. From the imperfective mówić.
Eating as a process. Jem obiad = I'm having dinner. Zjem obiad (from zjeść) = I'll eat it up.
To eat it up, all of it, done. Present-looking forms are future: zjem, zjesz, zje.
Having is a state, not an act that finishes, so there is no perfective mieć. "To get" (and then have) is a different verb: dostać.
Being is a state. Its future, będę, is not a perfective form but a separate imperfective future (chapter 5).

sets.title: Find the partner
sets.ask: Which is the other half of the pair?

items.q: The perfective partner of pisać is:
items.why: napisać adds only completion. Przepisać is "to copy out" and podpisać is "to sign" — prefixes that change the meaning, not just the aspect. Pisywać is a frequentative, not a partner.

items.q: The perfective partner of robić is:
items.why: zrobić is plain completion. Przerobić = to redo or to work through; dorobić = to make in addition. Those are new meanings.

items.q: The imperfective partner of zamknąć is:
items.why: -ykać / -knąć: zamykać / zamknąć. Odmykać is to unlock — the opposite action.

items.q: The imperfective partner of dać is:
items.why: dać / dawać is the clean pair. The others are different verbs: dodawać = to add, oddawać = to give back, podawać = to pass or to serve.

items.q: The perfective partner of brać is:
items.why: A suppletive pair — no shared root at all. Zabrać is to take away, wybrać is to choose, nabrać is to take on or to gather.

items.q: The perfective partner of widzieć is:
items.why: zobaczyć = to catch sight of, one act of seeing. A suppletive pair: the root -obaczyć is not the root of widzieć.

items.q: The imperfective partner of kupić is:
items.why: The -ić / -ować suffix pair. Dokupić = to buy in addition, wykupić = to buy out — new meanings.

items.q: The perfective partner of uczyć się is:
items.why: nauczyć się = to learn and now know it; the się stays. Without się, uczyć means "to teach", which is a different verb with its own pair.

items.q: Write the perfective partner of mówić.
items.why: powiedzieć — a suppletive pair: the roots share nothing. Powiem = I'll say it.

items.q: Write the imperfective partner of sprzedać.
items.why: sprzedawać / sprzedać — the same -awać / -ać shape as dawać / dać.

items.q: Write the perfective partner of zaczynać.
items.why: zaczynać / zacząć — the imperfective is the run-up, the perfective is the single starting point.

sets.title: Which half fits the sentence?
sets.ask: Choose the form the meaning needs

items.q: "I write to my mother every week." — which verb?
items.why: A habit, repeated — that is the imperfective's job. Piszę can mean "I write" as a habit, not only "I am writing". Napiszę would make it a single future act, and co tydzień contradicts that.

items.q: "I'll write the letter tomorrow (and it will be done)." — which verb?
items.why: One letter, one finished act — the perfective. Piszę list jutro is not impossible in speech (a plan, as a process), but for the plain future claim the perfective is the natural form.

items.q: "I was reading a book when he came in." — which verb?
items.why: A background process interrupted by a single event. The background is imperfective (czytałem), the interruption is perfective (wszedł). This contrast is the single most useful thing aspect does.

items.q: "I read the whole book yesterday." — which verb?
items.why: Całą (the whole of) makes it a finished quantity: the perfective. The imperfective czytałem would describe being in the middle of it, without saying you got to the end.

items.q: "He was eating when I phoned." — which verb?
items.why: The eating is the ongoing background (jadł), the phone call is the single completed event (zadzwoniłem). Note the past stem: jadł, not jedł.

items.q: "I'll drink it up and go." — which pair?
items.why: Both halves are single completed acts in the future: wypić (drink it up) and pójść (set off). Mixing a perfective future with an imperfective present (idę, which would mean "I'm going now") breaks the sequence.

An ongoing process: imperfective uczyć się, and the subject is in the genitive (polskiego) because uczyć się takes it. Nauczę się = I'll learn it (finished); uczę polskiego without się means "I teach Polish".

items.q: "I've learned it at last!" — which verb?
items.why: The result exists now, so the perfective: nauczyłem się (male speaker) / nauczyłam się (female). The imperfective would say you were studying, not that you got there.

items.q: Is it true that every prefixed verb is perfective?
opts: No — a prefix can make a secondary imperfective too
items.a: No — a prefix can make a secondary imperfective too
items.why: Prefix a verb and you usually get a perfective (pisać → napisać), but then a further suffix can make a new imperfective of it: napisać → napisywać (to write from time to time), przepisać → przepisywać. So a prefix alone does not decide it; the dictionary does.

items.q: Does aspect replace tense in Polish?
opts: No — they work together: aspect says whether it finished, tense says when
items.a: No — they work together: aspect says whether it finished, tense says when
items.why: Aspect and tense answer different questions. pisałem and napisałem are both past and both "I", but the first was a process and the second is a result. You need both pieces of information.

items.q: Why can być have a future form będę if it is imperfective?
opts: Because imperfective verbs form their future with będę + infinitive or past form
Because być is perfective after all
items.a: Because imperfective verbs form their future with będę + infinitive or past form
items.why: That is the compound future: będę pisać or będę pisał. Perfective verbs do not need it — they have a simple future (napiszę). Będę happens to be the future of być itself, which is a special case (chapter 5).

items.q: A learner says Wczoraj kupowałem chleb to mean "Yesterday I bought the bread (and now I have it)." What is off?
opts: The aspect: kupiłem is the finished purchase
items.a: The aspect: kupiłem is the finished purchase
items.why: Kupowałem means you were in the middle of buying / you used to buy. The plain report of a completed purchase is Kupiłem chleb. This is a classic: the past tense is not automatically imperfective.

items.q: Which sentence means "I'll be writing it (in the process) at eight"?
items.why: The compound future with the imperfective infinitive marks a process at a future moment. Napiszę would mean you will finish it; piszę is present; napisałem is past.

items.q: "I don't have time." — which is right?
items.why: mieć takes the accusative (czas), and the nie turns that object into the genitive: nie mam czasu. Same rule as nie mam biletu.

chapters.short: Six endings, four families, and the only present tense that a perfective verb does not have.

items.why: pisać → piszę. The -ać stem takes -ę for ja.
piszesz — the family ending for ty here is -esz, because this verb softens to pisz-.
piszemy — my always ends in -my; what comes before it is the stem plus a vowel.
piszą — the third person plural almost always ends in -ą.
czytam. The -ać family in its plainest form: -am, -asz, -a.
czytają — -ają. Compare piszą, where the stem is soft and takes only -ą.
mówię — the -ić family takes -ię. Mind the ę: mówię, not mówie.
mówisz — -isz after the soft stem. This is the marker of the whole -ić/-yć family.
mówią — -ą after the softened stem mówi-.
mam — the -m, -sz family has no ę at all: mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają.
mają — from the stem maj-, not mam-.
jestem — completely separate from the infinitive być. This is the first irregular verb (chapter 8).
są — a single short word, no jest- anywhere.
jem — the -m, -sz family: jem, jesz, je, jemy, jecie, jedzą.
jedzą — not jeją. The stem is jedz-.

items.q: Which verb belongs to the -am, -asz family?
items.why: mieszkać → mieszkam, mieszkasz. It is an -ać verb, and that family almost always goes to -am, -asz.

items.q: Which verb belongs to the -ę, -isz family?
items.why: dzwonić → dzwonię, dzwonisz. An -ić verb.

items.q: Which verb belongs to the -m, -sz family?
items.why: mieć → mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają. A closed, very old family: mieć, jeść, wiedzieć, dać and a few more.

items.q: pisać looks like an -ać verb but goes piszę, piszesz. Why?
opts: Its stem ends in a soft consonant, which shifts it into the -ę, -esz family
items.a: Its stem ends in a soft consonant, which shifts it into the -ę, -esz family
items.why: pisać has the stem pisz- (soft sz), and soft stems go -ę, -esz: piszę, piszesz. The same happens in skakać → skaczesz, płakać → płaczesz.

items.q: Which pair is not the same verb in two aspects?
opts: pracować / popracować — but popracować means "to work for a while"
items.a: pracować / popracować — but popracować means "to work for a while"
items.why: This one is subtler than it looks: popracować is perfective, but it means "to spend a while working", not simply "to finish working". Pracować has no plain completing partner. The other three are clean pairs.

items.q: A perfective verb like napisać has the forms napiszę, napiszesz…. What are they?
items.why: A perfective verb has no present, so these present-shaped forms carry future meaning: Napiszę list = I'll write the letter.

items.q: ___ piszemy list. — "We are writing a letter."
items.why: The ending -my is my. The pronoun is optional, but if a pronoun is there, it has to agree: My piszemy.
Oni is third person plural, so mówią. Mówi would be he/she/it; mówimy is we.

items.q: Czy ___ kawę? — "Do you drink coffee?" (to one person, informally)
items.why: Ty takes -sz: pijesz. Pije is he/she; pijecie is you plural.

items.q: Ja ___ z Łodzi. — "I am from Łódź."
items.why: jestem is ja. Note the case: after z meaning "from", the genitive — z Łodzi.

items.q: Gdzie ___? — "Where do you live?" (to one person)
items.why: mieszkasz — ty ending -sz on the stem mieszka-.

items.q: Oni nie ___ czasu. — "They have no time."
items.why: mają — third person plural of mieć. And because the verb is negated, the object is genitive: nie mają czasu.
czytacie — the wy ending is -cie.
idziemy — from the stem idzi-. The past of this verb is completely different: szliśmy.

items.q: Write the oni / one form of iść.
items.why: idą — one short word. Do not confuse it with the past szli.

chapters.short: The -ł- stem, gender that tells you who spoke, and the endings -em, -eś, -śmy, -ście.

sets.title: The -ł- stem
sets.ask: Build the past from the infinitive

items.q: The past tense of pisać is built on which stem?
items.why: Take the infinitive, drop -ć, add -ł: pisać → pisał. That is the whole rule for regular verbs; the endings go on this form.
pisał + -em → pisałem. The -ł stays.
pisała + -m → pisałam. The feminine uses -a- before the person ending.
czytaliśmy if the group includes at least one man; czytałyśmy if it is all women. Polish past plural makes that distinction, and the same split exists in the third person: czytali / czytały.
robił — the bare -ł form is third person singular masculine.
robiła — the feminine adds -a.
robili — masculine-personal plural. If the group has no men, it is robiły.
szedłem — the past stem of iść is szed-, unrelated to the present idę.
szła — no -e-. The masculine is szedł, the feminine szła.
jadł — not jedł. The past stem of jeść is jad-.
jedli — here the -e- is back, because the masculine-personal plural softens the stem.
byłeś — był + -eś. A woman would say byłaś.
mieliśmy — from mieli + -śmy.
wzięła — the ą of the infinitive becomes ę in the feminine and neuter. The masculine is wziął.

sets.title: Gender, and who is speaking
sets.ask: Which ending does the speaker need?

items.q: A man says "I was writing". Which?
items.why: -łem is the masculine form. A woman says pisałam. This is not about the object; it is about the speaker.

items.q: A woman says "We went". Which, if the group was all women?
items.why: poszłyśmy — all-female group. With at least one man in the group it is poszliśmy.

items.q: Which plural form is used for a group of women only?
items.why: Masculine-personal (at least one man) takes -li; everything else — women, children, animals, things — takes -ły. Polish calls these męskoosobowy and niemęskoosobowy.
Men are masculine-personal, so czytali. For a group of women or things it is czytały.

items.q: "The books were lying on the table." Which?
items.why: Books are not people, so they take the non-masculine-personal plural: leżały. Leżeli would need people — and men.

items.q: Where does the ending -śmy attach?
items.why: byliśmy — the ending fuses onto the -ł- form. The separated spelling -śmy byli exists but is formal and unusual in speech.

items.q: A woman says "I did it" — write ja of zrobić.
items.why: zrobiłam. The perfective changes nothing about the past endings — only about the meaning.

items.q: A man says "I didn't have time" — write ja of mieć in the past.
items.why: nie miałem / miałem. Note that the object after nie is genitive: nie miałem czasu.

sets.title: Past or present?
sets.ask: Which tense does the sentence need?

items.why: napisałem — past, perfective, and the masculine speaker ending -em. A woman would say napisałam.
piszę — present, imperfective, the process happening now.
The past of jeść is jadł-, so jadłeś (to a man) or jadłaś (to a woman). Zjesz? is "will you eat?"; jesz? is "are you eating?".
byłeś to a man, byłaś to a woman. Gdzie jesteś? is "where are you (now)?".

items.q: Which sentence uses the past correctly for a female speaker?
items.why: byłam — feminine -a- plus -m. Byłem would be a man speaking.

chapters.short: Two futures for imperfective verbs, one for perfective. Why będę pisać and napiszę are not the same promise.

items.q: "I will write the letter (and it will be done)." Which?
items.why: A perfective verb has a simple future made of its own present-shaped forms: napiszę. No będę is needed or wanted.

items.q: "I will be writing (in the process) all evening." Which?
items.why: An imperfective verb has no simple future, so it uses the compound future: będę + infinitive. The process is what lasts all evening.
będę takes an imperfective infinitive or past form. Będę napisać puts a perfective verb where only an imperfective can go — it has no meaning in Polish.

items.q: Będę pisał versus będę pisać: what is the difference?
opts: Meaning the same; the past-participle form can show gender and is commoner in speech
One is past, one is future
One is formal, one is rude
items.a: Meaning the same; the past-participle form can show gender and is commoner in speech
items.why: Both are correct compound futures. Będę pisał agrees with a male speaker and będę pisała with a female one; będę pisać is neutral about gender. The infinitive version is the easy default.

items.q: What is the future of być?
opts: będę, będziesz, będzie, będziemy, będziecie, będą
bym, byś, by, byśmy, byście, by
items.a: będę, będziesz, będzie, będziemy, będziecie, będą
items.why: będę is a complete future tense of its own. Bym, byś, by is the conditional (chapter 7), not the future.

opts: Jutro będzie padać. / Jutro będzie padało.
items.a: Jutro będzie padać. / Jutro będzie padało.
items.why: Weather verbs are impersonal and imperfective, so the compound future: będzie padać or będzie padało.

items.q: czytać — "I will read (be reading)", compound, neutral.
items.why: będę czytać — the compound future with the imperfective infinitive.
przeczytam — perfective, simple future. Notice it looks like a present tense; for a perfective verb, that is the future.

items.q: robić — "she will be doing it" (compound, feminine).
items.why: będzie robić or będzie robiła. The second shows the feminine subject twice: in będzie's third person and in the participle's -a.
zrobimy — simple future of the perfective.
będą — third person plural of the future of być. Do not confuse with są (present).
pójdę — perfective, so this present-shaped form is the future: I'll set off. For "I'll be walking about", the imperfective future is będę chodzić.
będą jeść or będą jedli. The compound future keeps the imperfective process.

items.q: Why is będę napisać list wrong?
opts: Będę needs an imperfective verb, and napisać is perfective
List is in the wrong case
items.a: Będę needs an imperfective verb, and napisać is perfective
items.why: The compound future marks an ongoing process, so it takes an imperfective infinitive: będę pisać. A perfective verb makes its own future without help: napiszę.

items.q: A learner says Jutro napiszę list to mean "Tomorrow I will be writing a letter (all morning)". What is off?
opts: The aspect: for a process in the future, use będę pisać
items.a: The aspect: for a process in the future, use będę pisać
items.why: Napiszę promises a finished letter, not a morning of writing. For the process, będę pisać list.

Będę móc przyszedł puts a past form after the infinitive and is wrong. The other three are all correct: będę mógł przyjść and będę móc przyjść are the two futures of “I will be able to come” (the first commoner in speech), and mogę przyjść means “I can come”.

items.q: "I'm going to Poland next year." Which is most natural?
opts: W przyszłym roku pojadę do Polski.
W przyszłym roku będę jechać do Polski.
W przyszłym roku jadę do Polski.
W przyszłym roku jechałem do Polski.
items.a: W przyszłym roku pojadę do Polski.
items.why: One journey, completed: the perfective pojadę. Będę jechać would describe being on the way; jadę is present or an arranged-now future.
będę is simply the future of być. Adding być after it is a double future and wrong.

chapters.short: Commands, requests, niech, and why Polish says proszę more often than it gives orders.

items.why: Pisz! — the imperative of an -ać verb usually ends in a soft consonant with no ending at all, or in -aj. Here: pisz.
Czytaj! — the -am family takes -aj in the imperative.
Rób! — a short, irregular imperative. Note the ó.
Idź! — the softening gives -dź. Plural: idźcie!
Mów! — an imperative with no ending, on the bare stem.
Daj mi! — from the imperfective dawać. Polish uses the imperfective for a plain request: Daj mi to. Dać itself has no ordinary imperative form in use.
Both exist: weź! (from the perfective, one act) and bierz! (from the imperfective). Weź is the everyday instruction.
Bądź! — the imperative of być. Bądź ostrożny to a man, bądź ostrożna to a woman.
Miej! — rare in speech, but the form is miej. The everyday phrase is Miłego dnia!, which needs no verb at all.
Czytajcie! — the plural imperative adds -cie to the singular.
Idźcie! — singular idź plus -cie.

items.q: How do you tell a stranger politely to come in?
items.why: Polish politeness is built on proszę + infinitive, not on a special imperative form. Wejdź! is fine between friends; to a stranger it is abrupt.

items.q: "Let him come in." Which is the third-person imperative?
items.why: niech + third-person form is how Polish says "let him / let them". Niech wejdzie = let him in; niech wejdą = let them in.
Chodźmy! is the first-person plural imperative — "let's go". Idziemy! states a fact ("we're going"), which in context can work as an invitation, but it is not an imperative.

items.q: How do you say "Don't do that!" to one person?
items.why: Negative commands take the imperfective: nie rób, not nie zrób. And the object after nie goes genitive: tego, not to.

items.q: Why is Nie zrób tego! odd?
opts: Negative imperatives use the imperfective: nie rób
items.a: Negative imperatives use the imperfective: nie rób
items.why: A prohibition is about an action to be avoided, not a result to be achieved, so Polish uses the imperfective: nie rób, nie pisz, nie mów. Positive commands can be either.
Nie pisz! — imperfective, as all negative commands are.

items.q: Which verbs have no imperative at all?
opts: Some impersonal and defective verbs, e.g. brakować, padać (of rain)
items.a: Some impersonal and defective verbs, e.g. brakować, padać (of rain)
items.why: You cannot command the rain, or command "to be lacking". Most ordinary verbs, perfective or not, do have imperatives — napisz! is perfectly good.

opts: Yes — positive commands can be perfective
No — only imperfective verbs have imperatives
Yes, but it means "you will write"
items.a: Yes — positive commands can be perfective
items.why: Napisz do mnie! = write to me (and do it). Perfective commands ask for a completed act; imperfective commands ask for a process or a habit. Only negative commands are restricted to the imperfective.

items.q: What does the ending -cie mark?
opts: A command to more than one person
items.a: A command to more than one person
items.why: czytaj → czytajcie, idź → idźcie. Politeness to one person is done with proszę + infinitive, or with niech pan/pani + verb.

items.q: "Please sit down" to one person, politely. Which?
items.why: Proszę usiąść is the standard polite form. Niech pan/pani usiądzie also works. Usiądź! is for friends and children.

chapters.short: bym, byś, by — politeness, hypotheses, and the conditional that polite Polish runs on.

items.q: "I would do it" — ja (a man), from robić.
items.why: Both are conditionals: zrobiłbym (perfective — I'd do it and it'd be done) and robiłbym (imperfective — I'd be doing it). For "I would do it" the perfective is the natural one.
zrobiłabym — the feminine -a- sits between the past stem and -bym.

items.q: "Would you help me?" — ty (to a man), from pomóc.
items.why: pomógłbyś — past stem pomógł plus -byś. To a woman: pomogłabyś.

items.q: "We would go" — my (a group with men), from pójść.
items.why: poszlibyśmy — past poszli + -byśmy.
pomogliby for a group with men, pomogłyby for a group without. The conditional keeps the past tense's gender split.

items.q: Which part carries the person in zrobiłbym?
items.why: -bym, -byś, -by, -byśmy, -byście, -by carry the person. The -ł- part carries the gender and the verb.

items.q: "I would like a coffee." Which is the standard polite form?
items.why: Chciałbym kawę (a man) / chciałabym kawę (a woman) is the polite request. Chcę kawę is perfectly correct but blunt — "I want a coffee".

items.q: "I would have done it" — a man. (The past conditional.)
items.why: zrobiłbym był — the past conditional, built with był at the end. It is literary and dated; in speech the plain conditional or the past does the job. Worth recognising, not worth using.

items.q: Which is the standard written form of "if I had time, I would read"?
opts: Gdy bym miał czas, czytał bym.
items.why: The conditional particle fuses onto the verb: czytałbym, and onto gdy: gdybym. The separated spelling (czytał bym) is also correct and common in careful writing, especially after a comma.

items.q: Where does bym normally sit in a sentence?
opts: Right after the verb, fused to it, or after a conjunction like gdy
items.a: Right after the verb, fused to it, or after a conjunction like gdy
items.why: zrobiłbym, gdybym, żebym. Bym is a clitic: it leans on the word before it, so it cannot stand alone at the start of a sentence.

items.q: "If I were you, I would go." Which?
items.why: Two things: być takes the instrumental (tobą), and both halves stay in the conditional (poszedłbym).

opts: "so that" / "in order to", and it takes the conditional
items.a: "so that" / "in order to", and it takes the conditional
items.why: Mówię powoli, żebyś zrozumiał — I speak slowly so that you understand. Żeby is że + by, fused, and the verb after it is conditional.

items.q: "I would like you to come" — write the conditional of przyjść for ty (a man).
items.why: przyszedłbyś — past przyszedł + -byś. To a woman: przyszłabyś.

opts: No — it is a mood: it says how real the action is, not when
Yes, it is a fourth tense
items.a: No — it is a mood: it says how real the action is, not when
items.why: Polish tryb przypuszczający is a mood. It can refer to the present, the future or the past: zrobiłbym to teraz / jutro. The tense still comes from context, as in English.

items.q: Why does Chciałbym sound more polite than Chcę?
opts: The conditional removes the demand — it makes the wish hypothetical
items.a: The conditional removes the demand — it makes the wish hypothetical
items.why: The same reason English says "I would like" rather than "I want". The conditional puts distance between the speaker and the demand, and Polish uses it constantly for requests: Czy mógłbyś…?, Chciałbym….

items.q: Which of these is not a correct negative request?
items.why: Double negation in the same clause is clumsy and unnatural here. The idiomatic way is wolałbym nie przychodzić (I'd rather not come) or czy mógłbym nie przyjść? (could I not come?).

items.q: "If it rains, we'll stay home." Which?
opts: Jeśli będzie padać, zostaniemy w domu.
Jeśli by padało, zostaniemy w domu.
items.a: Jeśli będzie padać, zostaniemy w domu.
items.why: A real, likely condition takes the ordinary future, not the conditional: jeśli będzie padać. The conditional gdyby padało would mark an unreal or unlikely condition: "if it were raining".

items.q: Which sentence is a proper unreal condition?
opts: Jeśli będę miał pieniądze, kupiłbym dom.
items.why: An unreal condition uses the conditional in both halves: gdybym miał… kupiłbym. Mixing a conditional if with a plain future breaks it.

chapters.short: The dozen verbs that break the patterns, taught as patterns of their own — including być, iść, jeść and wziąć.

items.why: jestem.
jesteś.
jest — one short word. Polish does not leave it out the way Russian does: To jest dom.
jesteśmy.
są — from a different root again.
byłam — the past is regular on był-, unlike the present.

items.q: "I am a programmer." Which case is programmer?
items.why: Jestem programistą. A profession, a role or an identity after być goes in the instrumental. An adjective does not: Jestem zmęczony (nominative).

items.q: "There is no coffee." Which is right?
items.why: nie ma + genitive is how Polish says "there is no / there isn't". It is a fixed phrase: nie ma kawy, nie ma czasu, nie ma problemu.

items.q: "I know where the station is." Which verb?
items.why: Wiem, gdzie jest dworzec. — a fact. wiedzieć takes a clause or o + locative: wiem o tym.
Znam Łódź dobrze. — familiarity with a place, a person or a language. Znam takes a plain accusative object.
Umiem pływać. — a learnt skill. Móc is about possibility or permission: Czy mogę wejść? — may I come in?
wiem — the present stem is wiem-, not wiedz-.
wiedzą — here the dz is back, and with -ą.
A language is something you znasz, and the object is accusative: Znasz polski? For a skill you use umieć: Umiem mówić po polsku.

sets.title: iść, chodzić, jechać, jeździć
sets.ask: On foot or by vehicle, one way or back and forth?

items.q: "I'm going to the shop now (on foot)." Which?
items.why: iść — one journey, on foot, happening now. Chodzę do sklepu means "I go to the shop (regularly)".

items.q: "I go to the shop every day (on foot)." Which?
items.why: chodzić is the repeated, back-and-forth partner of iść. The perfective pójść cannot carry codziennie.

items.q: "I'm going to Warsaw by train." Which?
items.why: jechać — one journey, by vehicle. The means of transport is instrumental: pociągiem.
idziemy.
szedł — completely different stem from the present.
jadę — present stem jad-. The past is jechał-.

items.q: Which verb would you use for a bus that runs on a route every day?
items.why: jeździć — repeated journeys by vehicle, a route, a habit. Jechać is one particular trip.
mam.
mają.
jesz.
jadł — the past stem has a, not e.
wezmę.
wziął — the masculine keeps the ą; the feminine is wzięła.
możesz.
mógł — the ó is only in the masculine singular; the feminine is mogła.
chcę.
dadzą — the -dzą ending is not predictable from da.
śpię — soft ś in the present, hard sp in the past (spał).
biorę — the -o- appears here and in biorą; elsewhere it is -e-: bierzesz.

chapters.short: Which case a verb takes, which preposition comes with it, and the verbs that take a case no English verb would suggest.

sets.title: Which case does the verb want?
sets.ask: Pick the case, not the ending

items.why: Szukam kluczy. The genitive even though English "look for" takes a plain object. Learn this one by heart: it is the classic rekcja trap.
Pomagam mamie. The person helped is the receiver — the dative's job.
Słucham muzyki. One of the verbs that resists the English pattern and takes the genitive.

items.q: interesować się (to be interested in) takes:
items.why: Interesuję się historią. The instrumental of interest — also in zajmować się.

items.q: bać się (to be afraid of) takes:
items.why: Boję się psów. Fear, like wanting and lacking, takes the genitive.
Dziękuję ci. The person thanked is the receiver: dative.
Jestem programistą. A role, a profession or an identity goes in the instrumental. An adjective does not: Jestem zmęczony.

items.q: uczyć się (to learn a subject) takes:
items.why: Uczę się polskiego. The subject being learnt is genitive; the reflexive się stays.
Potrzebuję pomocy. Needing is a kind of lacking, and lacking takes the genitive. (Older Polish allowed the accusative; the genitive is the modern standard.)

items.q: podobać się — "I like Łódź" — is built as:
opts: Łódź appeals to me — the thing is subject, the person dative
I like Łódź — the person is subject, the thing accusative
items.a: Łódź appeals to me — the thing is subject, the person dative
items.why: Podoba mi się Łódź. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person is dative. The same shape as Smakuje mi zupa and Podoba mi się ten film.
Negated direct object → genitive: biletu, not bilet.
gazeta changes from accusative gazetę to genitive gazety because of the nie.

items.q: "I don't see a car." — write the object: samochód.
items.why: Nie widzę samochodu. Genitive of samochód.

items.q: "I won't buy bread." — write the object: chleb.
items.why: Nie kupię chleba. Genitive of chleb.

items.q: Does the genitive-after-negation rule apply to all verbs?
opts: It applies to direct objects: a negated accusative object becomes genitive
Yes, every noun after nie goes genitive
items.a: It applies to direct objects: a negated accusative object becomes genitive
items.why: The rule is about the object: an accusative direct object turns genitive under negation. A dative (pomagam mamie) or an instrumental (interesuję się historią) does not change because of nie.
A quantity word — mało, dużo, trochę, a number — makes the object genitive, with no nie needed. Mam mało czasu.
czekać na + accusative: Czekam na autobus.
do + genitive. Sklep in the genitive is sklepu.
Events take na + accusative: na koncert, na spotkanie, na obiad. Places you go into take do + genitive.
myśleć o + locative. Ty in the locative is tobie.
zgadzać się z + instrumental: z tobą.
zależeć od + genitive: od ciebie.

items.q: "Thank you for the help" — complete Dziękuję za ___. (pomoc)
items.why: Dziękuję za pomoc. za + accusative here, and pomoc looks the same in the nominative and the accusative.

items.q: "I'm coming back from work" — complete Wracam z ___. (praca)
items.why: Wracam z pracy. z meaning "from" takes the genitive; praca → pracy.

chapters.short: The reflexive that changes meaning, the impersonal się, and the pronouns that ride along with a verb.

items.why: się here is the reflexive pronoun: the action goes back to the subject. Myję ręce without się means "I'm washing my hands".

opts: How do you spell that? — impersonal, no named doer
How is that written by me?
items.a: How do you spell that? — impersonal, no named doer
items.why: This is the impersonal się: the verb goes into the third person singular and no subject is named. English uses "you" or a passive for the same effect: Mówi się… = "people say…"

items.q: Uczę się polskiego. — what does się add here?
opts: It is part of the verb: uczyć się = to learn oneself (as opposed to uczyć = to teach)
items.a: It is part of the verb: uczyć się = to learn oneself (as opposed to uczyć = to teach)
items.why: uczyć = to teach; uczyć się = to learn. Drop the się and the meaning flips: the site's verb finder lists them as two verbs, because they are.
With a plural subject, się can mean "each other": Kochamy się = we love each other.

opts: It closes at eight — impersonal, about the shop
It is being closed by him
items.a: It closes at eight — impersonal, about the shop
items.why: Third person singular + się, no subject named: the shop closes. A very common way to say what happens without saying who does it.

items.q: "My name is Hammad." — complete Nazywam ___ Hammad.
items.why: Nazywam się Hammad. nazywać się is a verb with się built in; without it you would be naming someone else.

items.q: "I'm interested in history." — complete Interesuję ___ historią.
items.why: Interesuję się historią. Note the instrumental for the subject of interest.

items.q: Where does się normally go in a sentence?
opts: Right after the verb, before other pronouns
items.a: Right after the verb, before other pronouns
items.why: Myję się rano, Uczę się polskiego. Się is a clitic and leans on the verb; it does not usually begin a sentence.
Uczę studentów — I teach students. Uczę się polskiego — I learn Polish.

opts: to wash something versus to wash oneself
items.a: to wash something versus to wash oneself
items.why: Myję naczynia — I'm washing the dishes. Myję się — I'm washing myself.

items.q: bać się — can you say bać without się?
opts: No — bać się is the verb; without się it does not mean "to fear"
items.a: No — bać się is the verb; without się it does not mean "to fear"
items.why: Some verbs simply come with się as part of the dictionary form: bać się, podobać się, cieszyć się, śmiać się. Learn the się with them.

opts: podobać się = to appeal to ("I like it"); podobać alone is not used this way
items.a: podobać się = to appeal to ("I like it"); podobać alone is not used this way
items.why: Podoba mi się Łódź — Łódź appeals to me. The się is part of the verb, and the person is dative.

items.q: In the past tense, where does się go?
opts: After the past form: uczyłem się
Before the past form: się uczyłem
items.a: After the past form: uczyłem się
items.why: Uczyłem się polskiego, myła się. Się follows the verb form. Się uczyłem is possible in speech for emphasis but not the neutral order.

chapters.short: How pisac becomes napisać, przepisać, podpisać, wypisać: one root, a family of aspects and meanings.

items.q: pisać → napisać. What did na- do?
opts: Completed the action — it is now perfective
items.a: Completed the action — it is now perfective
items.why: na- here adds completion and no new direction: to write, and it is written.

opts: A new meaning: to sign (not simply to finish writing)
items.a: A new meaning: to sign (not simply to finish writing)
items.why: Podpisać is not the partner of pisać — it is a different verb. The partner is napisać. This is the trap of prefixes: they make words, not just aspects.

items.q: czytać → przeczytać. What does prze- add?
opts: Through: to read from start to finish
items.a: Through: to read from start to finish
items.why: prze- = through, across. The same sense in przejechać (drive past), przepisać (copy out).

items.q: pić → wypić. What does wy- add?
opts: Out, to the end: to drink it up
items.a: Out, to the end: to drink it up
items.why: wy- = out, to the end, thoroughly. Wyjeść is to eat out (the middle of something), wyspać się to sleep it off.

items.q: iść → wejść. What does w- add?
items.why: wejść = to go in. wyjść = to go out, dojść = to reach, odejść = to walk away.

items.q: dzwonić → zadzwonić. What does za- add?
opts: One completed call that reaches its goal
items.a: One completed call that reaches its goal
items.why: Zadzwonię do ciebie = I'll give you a call. Dzwonić is ringing as a process or a habit.

items.q: Which prefix turns robić into its plain perfective partner?
items.why: z- → zrobić. The simplest completing prefix in the language.

items.q: Which prefix turns słyszeć into "to hear (catch it)"?
items.why: u- → usłyszeć. U- marks a single completed act: usłyszeć, umyć, ujść.
od- = back, away: odpisać, oddać (give back), odejść (walk away).
prze- = through/across: przepisać, to write something across into a new place. Zapisać is to write down or to save.

items.q: Which word means "to write down, to note"?
items.why: zapisać — to write something down, or to save a file. Also zapisać się = to sign up.
wy- = out: wyjść, wyjechać (drive out), wynieść (carry out).
do- = up to, as far as: dojść do domu = to reach home. The preposition do is inside the prefix.
Podpisać — to sign, to write underneath.

items.q: Complete: w- + pić = ___ (to drink in, to absorb).
items.why: wpić is "to drink in, to absorb" (also wchłonąć). Less common than wypić, but built the same way.

chapters.short: The forms that turn a verb into an adjective, and where the verb sits in a Polish sentence.

opts: an active adjectival participle — "one who is doing"
items.a: an active adjectival participle — "one who is doing"
items.why: The active adjectival participle takes -ący from the present stem: robić → robiący. It behaves like an adjective: człowiek robiący zdjęcia — a man taking photos.
The passive adjectival participle takes -ny/-ony/-ty: robić → robiony. It is used with być for the passive: To jest robione ręcznie — it is made by hand.
The contemporary adverbial participle ends in -ąc: Czytam, pijąc kawę — I read while drinking coffee. It does not change for gender or number.
The verbal noun ends in -nie/-cie: robić → robienie, czytać → czytanie. It is a real noun and takes cases: uczenie się języków — the learning of languages.

items.q: Write the active adjectival participle of czytać.
items.why: czytający — present stem czytają- plus -cy.

items.q: Write the passive participle of czytać.
items.why: czytany — "read, being read".

items.q: Write the adverbial participle of czytać.
items.why: czytając — "while reading".

items.q: Write the verbal noun of czytać.
items.why: czytanie — "reading", as a thing.

items.q: What is the neutral Polish word order?
opts: Subject, verb, object — but flexible for emphasis
There is no order at all
items.a: Subject, verb, object — but flexible for emphasis
items.why: Marek czyta książkę is neutral. Książkę czyta Marek is the same facts with "it's the book that Marek is reading". Polish uses order for emphasis, not for grammar.

items.q: Where do clitics like się, mi and bym go?
opts: After the verb, in a fixed order among themselves
At the very end of the sentence
items.a: After the verb, in a fixed order among themselves
items.why: Podoba mi się, uczyłem się, zrobiłbym to. The order among clitics is fixed: bym before mi before się.

items.q: In a question like Czy Marek czyta książkę?, what is czy for?
opts: It marks a yes/no question with neutral order
items.a: It marks a yes/no question with neutral order
items.why: Czy at the start turns a statement into a yes/no question without changing the order. Without it, intonation does the job: Marek czyta książkę?

items.q: "I like this book." Which is the natural Polish?
items.why: podobać się reverses the English structure: the book is the subject, the person is dative. Lubię tę książkę is also correct and more direct — lubić takes the accusative.

items.q: Which is the neutral place for nie?
opts: At the end of the sentence
items.why: Nie mam czasu, Nie czytam gazety. In a compound past or future the nie goes before the whole verb phrase: Nie będę czytać.
